titleEn: 🎥 ‘The whole system is now more investable’: Reservoir makes the case for ag robotics
titleZh: Reservoir创始人：农业机器人“整个系统现在更具投资价值”
summaryZh: 在Salinas举办的Ruggedize大会上，Reservoir Farms创始人Danny Bernstein宣布与John Deere达成1000万美元研发合作，并阐述农业机器人为何正变得更值得投资。他指出，感知技术、边缘计算和AI的进步，加上现成的软硬件组件，使机器人开发周期缩短至6个月以内，且机器可跨作物、跨任务、跨行业复用。Reservoir VC正募集5000万美元基金，专注投资可跨领域发展的农业机器人初创企业。
featuredReason: 本文揭示了农业机器人投资逻辑的转变——从单一作物/任务到跨行业复合应用，以及Reservoir提供的“试验场+资金”模式，对智慧畜牧领域探索机器人自动化应用的从业者具有跨界借鉴意义。
contentFull:
When growers are testing new ag robots, they will usually tell you one of two things, observed Ben Palone at Western Growers at the inaugural Ruggedize conference at Reservoir Farms in Salinas: “They’ll say it’s alright, which means its working great, or it’s a piece of sh*t.”

Growers, said Verdant Robotics* CCO Curtis Garner, expect your machine “to just work. Bombproof, reliable, and if something breaks, swap it.” And they will always “buy reliability before they buy innovation,” added John Deere business integration manager Sean Sundberg.

While high-profile setbacks in the space have made some investors wary, advances in perception technologies, edge computing, AI and robotics combined with a growing stack of off-the-shelf hardware and software are helping startups build more flexible machines more quickly, said successive speakers.

And that, claimed Reservoir founder Danny Bernstein, means “the whole system is now more investable,” pointing to machines that are now being “assembled, prototyped and tested in less than six months” on a surprisingly tight budget. “There are very few companies who are really building the entire stack now. It’s just not really logical.”

Machines, meanwhile, are becoming more flexible, added Bernstein, who announced a $10m R&D partnership with John Deere at the event: “They’re able to compound to multiple crops, multiple tasks, multiple machines, and multiple industries.”

But they still need a lot of support in the early stages, says Reservoir, which is on a mission to accelerate the space through a combination of venture investment and hands-on practical support. Its 40-acre site in Salinas gives startups access to farmland, workshop space and a community of growers, founders, OEMs and technology companies, while its new Reservoir VC arm is raising $50 million to back early stage players in the segment.

In the first in a series of videos from the Ruggedize event, AgFunderNews (AFN) caught up with Bernstein (DB) to discuss why ag robotics is becoming more attractive to investors and how Reservoir is trying to shorten the path from prototype to commercial deployment.

[Disclosure: AgFunderNews’ parent company is an investor in Verdant Robotics.]

 

AFN: You’ve said that ag robotics is more investable now… why? What’s changed?

DB: Ag robotics is more investable because the underlying technology has allowed for significantly more degrees of freedom. We mean this in a literal sense in that machines are more flexible; they have more joints, they have more points of freedom, but also that the machines are smarter: there’s more happening on the device.

Another piece of that is that the underlying technology is now much more available off the shelf. There are very few companies who are really building the entire stack now. It’s just not really logical. You have open-source solutions like the robotics operating system (ROS). You have proprietary solutions from Google, Nvidia, and others. Those are all clearly very intertwined.

It was the case even 15, 20 years ago where you had to have your own cloud, and of course now you can pull that from Amazon or Nvidia. So you can stitch all these things together now, so that makes a difference.

And what that unlocks basically are these total addressable markets that can compound. So if agtech 1.0 in robotics was one crop, one task, and you were highly limited, someone would say, “Well, no one can invest in a strawberry harvester because even the best case scenario is they’re just a strawberry harvester.” But now that same company with a lot of the same stack, can become a cross-berry harvester, can pick romaine and iceberg and brassicas, and even can start to think about orchards.

That sort of sort of compound potential didn’t exist five or seven years ago. And those same machines can also begin to think about land management, about forestry… They’re originating in agriculture, which is one of the better markets for complex outdoor industries, and now they’re able to compound to multiple crops, multiple tasks, multiple machines, and multiple industries.

AFN: How are investors thinking about ag robotics? 

DB: We’re going to see a series of fundraising announcements. We saw one yesterday with TerraBlaster, for example, where Reservoir is an investor, and we should see a series of those now that I think will point to a really promising hot streak for agricultural robotics.

So, at a micro level, at a trend level, in the next six to 12 months, we’ll see some positive signals. But if we take a big step back and we think about why isn’t agricultural robotics at the first table of robotics, that’s a different question, and that fundamentally comes down to more systemic things.

If we compare it to defense, which we very often do, defense has two things. It has a buyer, which is of course the Department of War, which is a big buyer. It writes big checks and it writes big checks pretty early, and it also provides significant amounts of non-dilutive capital during the de-risking phase.

Agriculture doesn’t have either of those things right now. It doesn’t have the one big customer, the federal customer, nor does it have a federal de-risking mechanism, or even a state-level de-risking mechanism. And so, I would say for Reservoir, in terms of our agenda, building that system-level support around agriculture is one of the big unlocks that makes this sector more investable.

AFN: How deep is the pool of credible acquirers for some of these companies? And do firms need to have a broader addressable market that’s beyond ag to be of interest to these acquirers?

DB: We believe they do, and we invest across two segments. We invest in agricultural robotics, and those that we expect that those robotics companies can compound to other industries.

And that behavior exists, of course, in what we think of as traditional ag OEMs, where companies such as Deere and Kubota already operate across multiple outdoor industries. There are very few companies that are specific to ag OEMs.

The other area that we invest in and that we that we support is in the [tech] stack, what we call the rugged physical AI stack. This could be safety autonomy; this could be a navigation system; this could be various componentry. And that has a much broader aperture of potential acquirers that is dotted along Silicon Valley.

And so that’s where we think the space becomes more investable. We think about it not just as ag or agtech, but as rugged AI, rugged tech, and then the rugged AI stack, which can compound into Silicon Valley and beyond.

AFN: There is a lot of activity in precision spraying and weeding, but is harvesting proving a bigger challenge?

DB: Reservoir looks at three areas. We look at physics for chemical replacement. We look at AI and vision for chemical reduction or resource reduction using resources more precisely, and then a broad category, which is automation of the hardest to fill jobs, and that’s where harvest is very interesting.

Harvesting is a extraordinarily difficult engineering challenge. But we have a SAMI Robotics machine out there [near the entrance to Reservoir], which is arguably the most promising leafy greens harvester in the world right now.

The imperatives around harvest are more significant than ever before, and the relevancy around harvest automation is more significant than ever before.

AFN: You’ve argued that ag robotics companies need to be built around more realistic exit outcomes. But how much scope is there to lower burn rates and build more capital efficient models?

DB: So Reservoir has a company here called High Degree that is very capital efficient and raised just a little bit of venture capital. They built a full prototype here in about four months, and they’re already operating on commercial fields. So we do think that ag tech can be accelerated.

AFN: Give us the basics on Reservoir VC 

DB: Reservoir VC is an early-stage deep tech fund for rugged AI, and we recently brought in a new general partner to run the fund. Her name’s Nicola Kerslake. Nicola was part of a management company called Contain. We acquired Contain. Nicola was the founder of Indoor Ag-Con, so she’s got this really deep background in the space.

AFN: How much money has Reservoir VC got to work with?

DB: We recently wound down a $3 million proof of concept fund anchored by Taylor Farms, which is very common for first time funds. We made several investments out of that, including Farm-ng, which was acquired by Bonsai, and Bonsai is now doing great. We also invested in the pre seed round of Terrablaster, and they just raised a seed round, where we invested again, so that proof of concept fund has been a positive outcome.

These companies are really notable in the ag robotics space, and so it’s given us confidence to now build out a new vehicle.

So we started working on that as of June once Nicola came in, and the initial signal we’re getting is extraordinarily positive. It’s a $50 million dollar target and we’re getting a lot of interest from mission-aligned family offices, from producers, and a segment of investor that’s beginning to tiptoe into agtech that wants to see the future-proofing of farming through robotics.

AFN: At what stage is Reservoir VC investing?

DB: Reservoir VC will invest pre-seed and seed primarily. We are lead follow agnostic, but we’re probably a very good follow alongside a very traditional deep pocketed deep tech fund. That’s something that we did for example with TerraBlaster’s seed round, where we followed Khosla Ventures, with us being a complement, the ag strategic. Plus, we have a proving ground [at Reservoir Farms where firms can test their tech on crops], so we have we have this capability to be able to really support these companies, to be able to deeply integrate them into rural regions of California and beyond.

translationZh:
种植者在测试新型农业机器人时，通常会告诉你两种情况之一，Ben Palone在首届于Salinas Reservoir Farms举办的Ruggedize大会上观察道：“他们会说‘还行’，意思是它运行得很好，或者他们会说‘这玩意儿就是堆垃圾’。”

Verdant Robotics首席商务官Curtis Garner表示，种植者期望你的机器“能直接干活。坚固可靠，如果坏了，就换掉。”John Deere业务整合经理Sean Sundberg补充道，种植者总是“先买可靠性，再买创新”。

尽管该领域一些高调的挫折让部分投资者变得谨慎，但多位演讲者表示，感知技术、边缘计算、AI和机器人技术的进步，加上日益丰富的现成硬件和软件，正在帮助初创企业更快地构建更灵活的机器。

Reservoir创始人Danny Bernstein声称，这意味着“整个系统现在更具投资价值”，他指出，现在机器可以在“不到六个月的时间内”以“令人惊讶的紧凑预算”完成“组装、打样和测试”。“现在很少有公司真正在构建整个技术栈。这确实不太合乎逻辑。”

与此同时，机器正变得更加灵活，Bernstein补充道，他在活动上宣布了与John Deere的1000万美元研发合作：“它们能够复合应用于多种作物、多种任务、多种机器和多个行业。”

但Reservoir表示，它们在早期阶段仍然需要大量支持。Reservoir的使命是通过风险投资和手把手的实践支持相结合来加速该领域发展。其在Salinas占地40英亩的场地为初创企业提供了农田、工作坊空间以及一个由种植者、创始人、原始设备制造商（OEM）和科技公司组成的社区，而其新成立的Reservoir VC部门正在募集5000万美元，以支持该领域的早期玩家。

在Ruggedize活动系列视频的第一期中，AgFunderNews (AFN) 采访了Bernstein (DB)，讨论为什么农业机器人对投资者的吸引力越来越大，以及Reservoir如何努力缩短从原型到商业部署的路径。

[披露：AgFunderNews的母公司是Verdant Robotics的投资者。]

AFN：您说过农业机器人现在更具投资价值……为什么？发生了什么变化？

DB：农业机器人更具投资价值，是因为底层技术已经允许显著增加的自由度。我们说的既是字面意义上的，机器更灵活了；它们有更多的关节，有更多的自由点，但同时也意味着机器更智能了：设备上发生的事情更多了。

另一部分是，底层技术现在更容易从市场上直接获得。现在很少有公司真正在构建整个技术栈。这确实不太合乎逻辑。你有像机器人操作系统（ROS）这样的开源解决方案。你有来自Google、Nvidia等公司的专有解决方案。这些都明显紧密地交织在一起。

即使在15、20年前，你必须拥有自己的云，而现在当然你可以从Amazon或Nvidia那里获取。所以你现在可以把这些东西缝合在一起，这就产生了不同。

而这解锁的，基本上就是这些可以复合增长的总可寻址市场。所以，如果说机器人领域的农业科技1.0是单一作物、单一任务，而且你受到高度限制，人们会说，“嗯，没人能投资一个草莓收割机，因为即使最好的情况，它也只是一个草莓收割机。”但现在，同一家公司，用很多相同的技术栈，可以变成一个跨浆果收割机，可以收割长叶莴苣、冰山生菜和芸苔属蔬菜，甚至还可以开始考虑果园。

这种复合潜力在五到七年前是不存在的。而且同样的机器也可以开始考虑土地管理、林业……它们起源于农业，这是复杂的户外产业中较好的市场之一，现在它们能够复合到多种作物、多种任务、多种机器和多个行业。

AFN：投资者如何看待农业机器人？

DB：我们将看到一系列融资公告。我们昨天看到了TerraBlaster的例子，Reservoir是其中的投资者，我们应该会看到一系列这样的公告，我认为这将预示着农业机器人领域一个真正有希望的强劲时期。

所以，在微观层面，在趋势层面，在未来6到12个月，我们会看到一些积极的信号。但如果我们退一步，思考为什么农业机器人不在机器人的第一梯队，那是一个不同的问题，这根本上归结为更系统性的问题。

如果我们把它与国防相比，我们经常这样做，国防有两样东西。它有一个买家，当然是国防部，这是一个大买家。它开出大额支票，而且很早就开出大额支票，并且它在去风险阶段提供大量的非稀释性资本。

农业目前这两样都没有。它没有一个大客户，没有联邦客户，也没有联邦的去风险机制，甚至没有州级的去风险机制。所以，对于Reservoir来说，就我们的议程而言，围绕农业建立这种系统级的支持，是使这个行业更具投资价值的关键解锁因素之一。

AFN：这些公司可信的收购方池子有多深？公司是否需要拥有超越农业的更广泛的可寻址市场，才能引起这些收购方的兴趣？

DB：我们相信它们需要，而且我们在两个领域进行投资。我们投资于农业机器人，并且我们期望这些机器人公司能够扩展到其他行业。

这种行为当然存在于我们认为是传统农业OEM的公司中，例如Deere和Kubota这样的公司已经在多个户外行业运营。很少有公司是专门针对农业OEM的。

我们投资和支持的另一个领域是[技术]栈，我们称之为坚固的物理AI栈。这可能是安全自主；可能是导航系统；可能是各种组件。这拥有更广泛的潜在收购方，遍布硅谷。

所以这就是我们认为这个领域变得更值得投资的地方。我们不仅仅把它看作农业或农业科技，而是看作坚固AI、坚固技术，然后是坚固AI栈，它可以扩展到硅谷及其他地方。

AFN：在精准喷洒和除草领域有很多活动，但收获是否是一个更大的挑战？

DB：Reservoir关注三个领域。我们关注用于替代化学品的物理方法。我们关注用于减少化学品或资源消耗的AI和视觉，更精确地使用资源，然后是一个广泛的类别，即最难填补的岗位的自动化，这就是收获非常有趣的地方。

收获是一个极其困难的工程挑战。但我们在[Reservoir入口附近]有一台SAMI Robotics机器，它可以说是目前世界上最有前途的绿叶蔬菜收割机。

围绕收获的紧迫性比以往任何时候都更加重要，围绕收获自动化的相关性也比以往任何时候都更加重要。

AFN：您认为农业机器人公司需要围绕更现实的退出结果来构建。但是，在降低烧钱率和建立更资本高效的模型方面有多大空间？

DB：Reservoir这里有一家叫High Degree的公司，它非常资本高效，只筹集了一点点风险投资。他们在这里大约四个月内就建造了一个完整的原型机，并且已经在商业田地上运营了。所以我们确实认为农业科技是可以加速的。

AFN：请介绍一下Reservoir VC的基本情况。

DB：Reservoir VC是一个专注于坚固AI的早期深度科技基金，我们最近引入了一位新的普通合伙人（GP）来管理该基金。她叫Nicola Kerslake。Nicola曾是一家名为Contain的管理公司的一员。我们收购了Contain。Nicola是Indoor Ag-Con的创始人，所以她在该领域有非常深厚的背景。

AFN：Reservoir VC有多少资金可以运作？

DB：我们最近结束了一个由Taylor Farms领投的300万美元的概念验证基金，这对首次募资的基金来说很常见。我们用这笔基金进行了几项投资，包括Farm-ng，它被Bonsai收购了，而Bonsai现在做得很好。我们还投资了Terrablaster的种子前轮，他们刚刚完成了种子轮，我们又进行了投资，所以那个概念验证基金取得了积极成果。

这些公司在农业机器人领域确实很知名，所以这给了我们信心去建立一个新的投资工具。

所以从六月Nicola加入后我们就开始着手准备，我们得到的初步信号是非常积极的。这是一个5000万美元的目标，我们收到了很多来自使命一致的家庭办公室、生产商以及一类开始涉足农业科技、希望通过机器人技术实现农业未来保障的投资者的浓厚兴趣。

AFN：Reservoir VC在什么阶段进行投资？

DB：Reservoir VC主要投资于种子前和种子轮。我们对领投或跟投没有偏好，但我们可能非常适合作为传统资金雄厚的深度科技基金的优秀跟投者。例如，我们在TerraBlaster的种子轮中就是这样做的，我们跟投了Khosla Ventures，我们是作为补充，作为农业战略投资者。此外，我们有一个试验场[在Reservoir Farms，公司可以在那里测试他们的技术]，所以我们有能力真正支持这些公司，能够将它们深度整合到加州及其他地区的农村地区。

AFN：请介绍一下您的有限合伙人（LP）基础。

DB：我们有一个非常深度科技，甚至有点极客风格的LP基础，所以在某些方面

AFN：投资者如何看待农业机器人？

DB：我们会看到一系列融资公告。比如昨天就有一个TerraBlaster的案例，Reservoir是其中的投资者。我认为接下来会陆续看到一系列这样的公告，这将预示着农业机器人领域将迎来一波非常令人振奋的热潮。

所以，在微观层面、在趋势层面，未来6到12个月，我们会看到一些积极信号。但如果我们退一步思考，为什么农业机器人没有进入机器人的第一梯队，那就是另一个问题了，这根本上归结为更系统性的因素。

如果我们拿它和国防领域比较——我们经常这样做——国防有两个优势。它有一个买家，当然是国防部，这是一个大买家。它开出大额支票，而且相当早就开出大额支票，同时它还在去风险阶段提供大量非稀释性资本。

农业目前两者都不具备。它既没有那个大客户——联邦客户，也没有联邦层面的去风险机制，甚至没有州层面的去风险机制。所以，对Reservoir来说，就我们的议程而言，围绕农业建立这种系统层面的支持，是让这个行业更具投资价值的关键解锁因素之一。

AFN：对于这些公司来说，可信的收购方池子有多深？公司是否需要拥有超越农业的更广泛的可寻址市场，才能引起这些收购方的兴趣？

DB：我们认为确实如此，我们投资于两个细分领域。我们投资农业机器人，同时我们也预期这些机器人公司能够扩展到其他行业。

这种行为当然也存在于我们所说的传统农业OEM中，像迪尔和久保田这样的公司已经在多个户外行业运营。专门针对农业OEM的公司非常少。

我们投资和支持的另一个领域是技术栈，我们称之为“ rugged physical AI stack”（坚固型物理AI技术栈）。这可能是安全自动驾驶，可能是导航系统，也可能是各种组件。这个领域有更广泛的潜在收购方，遍布硅谷。

所以这就是我们认为这个领域变得更具投资价值的地方。我们不只把它看作农业或农业科技，而是看作坚固型AI、坚固型技术，以及能够扩展到硅谷及更远地方的坚固型AI技术栈。

AFN：精准喷洒和除草领域有很多活动，但收获环节是否是一个更大的挑战？

DB：Reservoir关注三个领域。我们关注用于化学替代的物理技术，关注用于减少化学品或资源消耗、更精准使用资源的AI和视觉技术，还有一个广泛的类别，即最难填补岗位的自动化，而收获环节就在这里非常有趣。

收获是一个极其困难的工程挑战。但我们在Reservoir入口附近有一台SAMI Robotics的机器，它可以说是目前世界上最有前途的叶菜收割机。

围绕收获的紧迫性比以往任何时候都更加显著，收获自动化的相关性也比以往任何时候都更加重要。

AFN：你曾提出，农业机器人公司需要围绕更现实的退出结果来构建。但降低烧钱率、建立更资本高效的模型，空间有多大？

DB：Reservoir旗下有一家叫High Degree的公司，它非常资本高效，只筹集了很少的风险投资。他们大约四个月就在这里建成了完整的原型机，而且已经在商业农田上运营了。所以我们确实认为农业科技是可以加速的。

AFN：请介绍一下Reservoir VC的基本情况。

DB：Reservoir VC是一家专注于坚固型AI的早期深度科技基金，我们最近引入了一位新的普通合伙人管理基金。她叫Nicola Kerslake。Nicola曾是一家名为Contain的管理公司的一员。我们收购了Contain。Nicola是Indoor Ag-Con的创始人，所以她在该领域有非常深厚的背景。

AFN：Reservoir VC有多少资金可以运作？

DB：我们最近结束了一个由Taylor Farms锚定的300万美元的概念验证基金，这对首次成立的基金来说非常常见。我们用这笔基金做了几项投资，包括Farm-ng，该公司已被Bonsai收购，Bonsai现在发展得很好。我们还投资了Terrablaster的种子前轮，他们刚刚完成了种子轮融资，我们又参与了投资，所以这个概念验证基金取得了积极成果。

这些公司在农业机器人领域非常引人注目，因此给了我们信心去建立一个新的基金载体。

所以从6月份Nicola加入后我们就开始着手这项工作，我们得到的初步信号非常积极。目标是5000万美元，我们收到了很多来自使命导向型家族办公室、生产商以及一部分开始试探性进入农业科技、希望通过机器人技术实现农业未来保障的投资者的浓厚兴趣。

AFN：Reservoir VC在什么阶段进行投资？

DB：Reservoir VC主要投资于种子前和种子轮。我们是领投跟投皆可，但我们可能非常适合作为传统资金雄厚的深度科技基金的跟投方。比如在TerraBlaster的种子轮中我们就这么做了，我们跟投了Khosla Ventures，我们作为补充，提供农业战略价值。此外，我们在Reservoir Farms有一个试验场，企业可以在那里测试他们的技术在作物上的表现，所以我们有能力真正支持这些公司，将他们深度融入加州及其他地区的农村区域。

AFN：请介绍一下你们的LP基础。

DB：我们有一个非常深度科技、甚至有点极客风格的LP基础，所以在某种程度上——
